title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 27-32
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of letting go of mental attachments and embracing the present moment, aligning with teachings from various Buddhist traditions that value joy, ease, and calm as keys to achieving enlightenment. Through the practice of Zazen, or sitting meditation, we can cultivate awareness and understanding by releasing thoughts and distractions, finding freedom from attachment and ego. By tuning into our physical bodies and being open to the impermanence of all things, we can live a more authentic and compassionate life.

sentences.text: **Joden Bob Rose:** The story I'd like to tell is about Myozen Joan Amaral, who I mentioned was the one who brought me to practice when I met her at the San Francisco Zen Center.
We visited on a Zoom call the other day, and she was reflecting on how unusual it is that this poem of [unclear: "sure-do's"] has only recently arisen in our view.

Tigin Dan Layton, who first translated this poem, didn't translate it until 1985, and it wasn't published in a book until the year 2000, 15 years later, as an appendix to Hong Ji's Cultivating the Empty Field.
We were pondering this, and she proposed a thought.

As Ben Connolly points out, there's a lot of emphasis in this poem on relaxation and ease, and her sense was that perhaps that didn't fit the stern notion of Zen that we've been presented with, and certainly in the Japanese tradition a much harder-line sense of practice.
It really raised for both of us a classic question.
This poem is now recited at the Minneapolis Zen Center and at the North Shore Zen Center, where Myozen Joan is the guiding teacher.
It's been incorporated as part of the liturgy.
I think it raised a really interesting question about spiritual life: when does a text become liturgy?
When is it an apocryphal text?
When is it heretical?
And when is it just forgotten entirely?
It's really interesting that a text written in 780 or so finally comes to us now and has not been part of the public arena for all these many years.
It's just something to really think about, as we've all found this text so effective and so timely in our practice.
So, the final installment of a couple of Shurdu [unclear: "and counter"] dialogues.
*When Monk Baotong first came to study with Master Shurdu, the master asked him, "Can you show me your mind?"
Baotong replied, "That which distinguishes your words is my mind."
The master shouted and drove him away.
Later Baotong again approached the master and said, "If what I said last time isn't my mind, then what is?"
The master said, "Without raising your eyebrows or blinking your eyes, show me your mind."
Baotong said, "I don't have any particular mind to show you."
The master said, "Originally you do have a mind, so why say you don't?
If you deny it, it's just lying."
At this Baotong had a realization.*
*Another time the same monk Baotong asked Master Shurdu, "An ancient said that it's mistaken to believe in the way, and also mistaken to believe that there is not a way.
I ask the master to please explain."
Master Shurdu said, "There's not a thing here.
What do you want me to explain?"
Baotong was silent.
Then the master said, "Throw away your throat, mouth and lips and let's see what you can say."
Baotong said, "There's nothing left."
The master said, "If that's really so, then you've entered the gate."*
And the last encounter dialogue, which is spot on for tonight, especially the last couple of lines in the poem:
*A monk named Huilang once asked Master Shurdu, "What is the awakened one?"
The master said, "You don't have an awakened mind."
Huilang, dejected, said, "I'm just human.
I know I run around and have all kinds of ideas."
The master said, "Active people with ideas still have awakened mind."
Huilang said, "Then why don't I?"
The master said, "Because you're not satisfied to be just human."
Huilang had a deep realization.*
Let me read that again.
*A monk named Huilang once asked Master Shurdu, "What is the awakened one?"
The master said, "You don't have an awakened mind."
Huilang, dejected, said, "I'm just human.
I know I run around and have all kinds of ideas."
The master said, "Active people with ideas still have awakened mind."
Huilang asked, "Then why don't I?"
The master said, "Because you're not satisfied to be just human."*
So, the final six lines of the poem, the final stanza as it's constructed in the translation:
*Let go of hundreds of years and relax completely.
Open your hands and walk, innocent.
Thousands of words, myriad interpretations are only to free you from obstructions.
If you want to know the undying person in the hut, don't separate from this skin bag here and now.*
In the Heart Sutra, we chant the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths.
We chant no suffering, no cause, no cessation, no path.
And then we say no knowledge and no attainment.
With nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajnaparamita, and thus the mind is without hindrance.
Without hindrance, there is no fear.
What better proposition for innocence?
No fear.
Couple that with Shurdu's earlier "this monk doesn't understand at all," and his response to the question, what is the essential meaning of the Buddha Dharma?
Not attaining, not knowing.

And so now at this point in the poem, we're given our instructions for how to set forth: to get up off our cushion in profound sincerity, relaxed, having let go of our mental encumbrances, and now presenting ourselves to the suffering world that we have vowed to offer our help to heal, even while we recognize our own inability to complete the task before us.
Let go of hundreds of years and relax completely.
Open your hands and walk innocent.

When we chant "all my ancient twisted karma from beginningless greed, hate, and delusion, born through body, speech, and mind, I now fully avow," we are letting go of those hundreds of years, those kalpas of what has preceded us, to be in this very moment, right now.
Shoto Hirado Roshi reminds us that when karma ripens and all things come to be, being here in this moment, we are able to be with what is, to respond to what is.
Just this is it, in this body, right now.
One of my guiding poets, as I mentioned in my way-seeking mind, Charles Olson, has a line that has stuck with me and that really reflects on this.
He says, "I have had to learn the simplest things last, which made for difficulties."
Sometimes we forget that the factors of relaxation and joy are key points of our teachings.
Relax is another word for ease.
One of the teachings that Tim brought forward early in my practice was the 37 steps of the Bodhipaksha Dharma.
In the Factors of Enlightenment, in that 37-step recitation, the third step is joy, and the fourth is lightness and ease, and Samadhi and equanimity follow after that.
We chant often the Enmei Jukku Kanangyo, the lines Bupo Soen, Jo Raku Gajo, which translate as affinity with Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; constancy, ease, assurance, and purity.

Roshi Aitgen, in his essay on Enmei Jukku Kanangyo, tells us that with our affinity with the three treasures, with Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, we simultaneously, as a result, have constancy, ease, assurance, and purity, which he points out are the four attributes of nirvana.
The factor of rapture or joy is both happiness and satisfaction felt in the mind as well as in the body, and the lightness and the waves of bliss felt in the body.
The factors of calm and serenity, quietness or tranquility, naturally follow from that joy and lead then to concentration, to Samadhi.
And so it turns out that when our joy and tranquility are developed, we are just the opposite of restlessness and remorse.
Our lives are in a very different mode.

One of my fondest moments, and for others who were with us in Japan with Mountain Rain, was a Dharma talk that Hoitsu Suzuki gave us in the Dharma Hall at Rinso Inn, and the Dharma talk was on the theme "to practice with joy."
A text that I came across early in my studies is by Kosho Uchiyama.
It's a book called Opening the Hand of Thought, and given the reference to Hannah, she'll put it on the notice afterwards, so if you want to follow up on this.

Kosho Uchiyama, who's actually a part of the lineage that Ben Connolly comes from, tells us that this opening the hand of thought is an attitude of refraining from all mental fabrication, of recognizing that there is no possible reality other than that which is right now, the absolute and undeniable present moment.

Or as he says, dwelling here and now in this reality, letting go of all the accidental things that arise in our minds is what I mean by opening the hand of thought: to be free from ideas we make up in our heads, to be totally present with what he calls the reality that can't be grasped or understood through reason or intellect.
This very ungraspability is what is absolutely real about things.
Zazen is our way to train our minds to open the hand of thought and simply refrain from grasping each thought as it inevitably arises and floats away, as we don't grasp for it or try to follow it.
And we bring that training effortlessly to our moment-by-moment lives off the cushion as best we can, because we all know we have moments where we're not fully paying attention.
But the cushion gives us a great reference for how we live our life moment by moment.
One night I came up to the Zendo and I saw a car that had a bumper sticker that says, "Don't believe everything you think."
Uchiyama refers to Dogen's dropping off of body and mind as exactly this opening the hand of thought, fully letting go.

In our studies over the past weeks we have entered this poem, and it embodies our practice and places us as bodhisattvas without doubt, practicing in the heart of the entire world, innocent, not understanding at all, no longer working to get free, intimate with our ancestors and Buddha nature.
And we are urged to persist in our efforts to bind the grasses of our mind and body hut, and not to give up, to just keep going.

Sometimes as I'm watching the screen, one of the great puns and realities that pops up is that bodhisattva comes up as "bodhisattva," and I think that's a really nice little signature for reminding ourselves what we're all involved in.
*Thousands of words, myriad interpretations are only to free you from obstructions.*
My farmer friend Dave Headland has a family of Mexican folks who've been working for him for many, many years, and one of them, David Rodriguez, has a saying.
He says, "too lata, too lata" something.
And when I read this line I thought, too lata books, too lata books.
All those books, all those Dharma talks, all the conversations, the arguments, the disputations, the mentations, as they're called in some of our texts, all that thinking, to what end?
We humans, those of us who choose to live a full life, have an endless curiosity, like a fish swimming in the sea, in the merciful ocean of the Buddha's way.
Each taste, each sip makes us long for another, and they're all fingers pointed at the moon.
Another poet that I've referred to often in my life, and a friend who lived in Burlington, Washington for part of his life, was Ed Dorn.

He wrote a very funny, long philosophical poem called The Gunslinger, and there's a line in there that's always stuck with me, where the gunslinger says, "You want to know what something means after you've seen it and after you've been there, or were you out during that time?"
So we put away the texts and find that place of calm and knowing without thinking when we sit.
Then we get up, we engage the world, we sit again and we keep going.
We don't give up.
We practice continuously, from cushion to kitchen, from slouching to sleeping.
It is all practice.
*If you want to know the undying person in the hut, don't separate from this skin bag here and now.*
My Dharma companion Paul Hanson gave an alternative little translation of this one line, something like, "How can you separate yourself or get away from this skin sack and still have a day?"
In the Dhammapada, the kind of core teachings of the Buddha, the Buddha says:
*Vigilance is the realm of immortality.
Negligence is the realm of death.
People who are vigilant do not die.
People who are negligent are as if dead.*

Thomas Cleary, the translator, says that when the Buddha says the vigilant do not die, it's because they are attuned to objective reality, which is eternal, not fixated on the subjective delusions in their minds, which are temporal.

One of the texts that Shidu clearly had in mind and was familiar with, because it was written by Sheng San, the third ancestor, so not having come from India but right there from China, is the Xin Xing Ming, Trust in Mind.
It opens with the lines "The great way is not difficult for those who have no preferences."
Red Pine translates that as "The way isn't hard to find, just avoid choosing."
And later on in this poem, lines 38 to 39 are a passage that reflects directly on our skin bag.
So I'll read two translations, one from Musong, which is the translation I primarily looked at, and one from Red Pine.
*If you wish to move in the one way, do not dislike even the world of senses and ideas.
Indeed, to accept them fully is identical with true enlightenment.*
Or an alternative translation:
*Those who take the path of oneness give the dust of sensation no thought.
Giving the dust of sensation no thought, this is the same as enlightenment.*
That is, we use our senses to experience reality that includes our empty mind.
And this empty mind takes note of all it perceives and is guided by its sensing needs.
We understand that our senses themselves can be a skillful tool to discern the nature of reality.
We are, after all, human animals.
And compared to other animals, we have the freedom, if we choose, to be prisoners of our skeleton and brain systems, or to use our brains and bodies to understand ourselves skillfully.
We chant Dogen's Fukanzazengi:
*You have gained the pivotal opportunity of human form.
Do not use your time in vain.
You are maintaining the essential working of the Buddha way.*
He tells us elsewhere that in Buddha Dharma, body and mind are not separate.
That is why they are called body-mind.
He further tells us that since Buddha ancestors are body and mind as one:
*One phrase or two are the Buddha ancestors, warm body-mind.
Their body-mind comes forth and realizes your body-mind.
At the very moment of realization, this realization comes forth and realizes your body-mind.
This life realizes the life of many lifetimes.
By becoming a Buddha and becoming an ancestor, you go beyond Buddha and go beyond ancestor.*

Our bodies, our lives, are the unique opportunity both to become Buddha, to go beyond Buddha, that is, to further and continue the Buddha Dharma, and to fully acknowledge simultaneously our mortality and our undying nature.
"If you want to know the undying person in the hut," as this couplet opens, poses the question to each of us.
If you want to know, then this is a choice: to enter practice or not, to remain a sentient being or to recognize our Buddha nature and take on that responsibility.

It's making that choice to sit, to take our vows, to practice with an open, generous, caring, and joyful heart, and through that effort to know, to embody, to enact that undying person in the hut, in our own self-created hut.

Our bodies at this moment are the entire universe, the universe where and when, 14 billion years ago, atoms have congealed in this form to provide each of us the opportunity to practice and to bring our intention to be compassionate and mindful at all times.
What a miracle, what a responsibility.
So I'm going to close with a little prayer that is part of our liturgy and part of our heritage, called the five remembrances.
*I am of the nature to grow old, there is no way to escape growing old.
I am of the nature to have ill health, there is no way to escape ill health.
I am of the nature to die, there is no way to escape death.
All that is dear to me and everyone I love are of the nature to change, there is no way to escape being separated from them.
My actions are my only true belongings.
I cannot escape the consequences of my actions.
My actions are the ground upon which I stand.*

So we're going to go out into breakout rooms, and the question I've raised for all of us tonight is, and Hannah will have this typed out as well: How do you stay one with your skin and live your practice?
What difficulties do you encounter and how do you respond?
How do you stay one with your skin and live your practice?
What difficulties do you encounter and how do you respond?

We'll have a breakout room for about 20 minutes or so and then come back, and just have prepared a line or a couple of words to provide to the rest of us, so we can have a sense of how these final stanzas have precipitated some thoughts and some feelings on your part about how you make this practice real for yourselves.
Thank you.
**Participant:** I just check with my skin bag and ask it, what does my skin bag need?
And often it's something like food, or just a stretch, or get away from the computer.
There's usually something that at least will distract me from the malaise of the skin bag at the moment.
Things do shift into more openness, more groundedness.

In the mornings I like to take a little time with my skin bag and find my pulse and just listen to my pulse for a few moments, and I recognize that the pulse is happening not because of me, you know, nothing I'm doing, and I'm thankful for that.
I don't know, I just feel a sense of humbleness and gratitude and strength.
**Joden Bob Rose:** We have time for one more.
**Participant:** Okay, this wasn't discussed in the breakout, but when Mari was talking about the mindfulness bell going off, that reminded me of another tradition entirely.
You know, in Islam, the haunting call to prayers five times a day, and then they get together and do their prayers, which could be a contemplative type of experience.
I've always found that a beautiful thing, and coming back purposely five times a day would be great.
I've never done it, but it sounds pretty cool.
Thank you all for your
**Joden Bob Rose:** thoughtful comments.
What Hannah and I will do before next week's class is send out a couple of questions, and basically I won't be talking about the poem.
I have some questions that would be more of a round table.
We'll probably break out into smaller groups as well, but we have walked through these 32 lines and we could start all over again, but we're not going to.
I really appreciate all of your thoughts, and you're helping me understand how this poem has resonated with you, so thank you very much.
I just want to toss in a reminder or two about next week: the sesshin will start next Thursday evening, all day Friday, Saturday and into Sunday.
If you can't come to the sesshin, you could come to the Dharma talks, myself on Friday and Bob on Saturday, at 11:10 in the morning.

And then most especially, mark in your calendar, consider if you can come to the Shuso's Dharma inquiry ceremony a week from Sunday, when we get to explore the Dharma in a little different way with our Shuso, so Sunday at 11.
That's all on the website.
So just here it is, you know, end of practice period around the corner.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
